title: Where to See Wild Elephants in India: A Guide to the Best Wildlife Sanctuaries
excerpt: From Karnataka's Kabini riverbanks to Kerala's Periyar Lake, India shelters more than 60 percent of the world's wild Asian elephants across a network of reserves tailor-made for wildlife safaris.
body:
• India is home to an estimated 22,446 wild Asian elephants — more than 60 percent of the global population — according to the country's first DNA-based census released in 2025.
  • Karnataka's Nagarhole and Bandipur reserves, connected within the Nilgiri Biosphere, support roughly 6,000 elephants and offer both jeep and boat safaris.
  • Kerala's Periyar Wildlife Sanctuary and Wayanad provide unique boat-based sighting experiences; Assam's Kaziranga adds elephant encounters alongside one-horned rhinos.
  • The dry season from October to April is the optimal window, when receding water drives herds into the open near waterholes and riverbanks.

India's relationship with the Asian elephant runs deep — culturally, ecologically and spiritually. The country harbors the largest share of the world's remaining wild Asian elephants, an endangered species whose habitat continues to shrink under pressure from infrastructure expansion and human-elephant conflict. A landmark DNA-based census by the Wildlife Institute of India, released in October 2025, estimated the population at 22,446, establishing a new scientific baseline after earlier direct-count methods put the figure closer to 29,000.

For visitors from the diaspora looking to reconnect with India's natural heritage, few experiences rival watching a herd of wild elephants cross a forest clearing at dawn. Here are the reserves where those encounters are most likely.

Nagarhole and Bandipur: Karnataka's Elephant Heartland

Karnataka supports the largest wild elephant population of any Indian state — roughly 6,013 animals, according to the 2025 census. The twin reserves of Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi National Park) and Bandipur Tiger Reserve sit at the core of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, a 5,520-square-kilometer landscape that also includes Tamil Nadu's Mudumalai and Kerala's Wayanad.

Nagarhole's standout draw is the Kabini River boat safari. For much of the year the Kabini expands into a reservoir, but as the dry season peaks between February and April, the water retreats and grassy banks become a magnet for elephant herds. The Kabini River Lodge, operated by Jungle Lodges and Resorts, runs morning and evening boat trips where sightings of elephants bathing and feeding are common. On land, jeep safaris weave through dry deciduous forest where roughly 2,500 elephants share space with around 150 tigers, leopards, gaur and dholes.

Bandipur, 80 kilometers south of Mysuru, offers similar terrain and restricts safaris to a controlled zone along the Mysuru–Ooty road. The dry months yield the best sightings as animals converge on shrinking waterholes.

Periyar Wildlife Sanctuary: Elephants at the Water's Edge

Set in Kerala's Western Ghats around the scenic Periyar Lake, this 925-square-kilometer sanctuary is one of India's most accessible elephant-watching destinations. The Kerala Forest Department runs boat cruises on the lake, and elephants are regularly spotted on the banks — bathing, drinking or simply wading through the shallows. The surrounding forests shelter tigers, leopards, wild boar and over 260 bird species.

Kerala holds an estimated 2,785 wild elephants. Periyar is open from October to June, with the December-to-April window offering the clearest weather and most reliable sightings. The sanctuary's proximity to Thekkady town makes logistics straightforward — a factor that matters for visitors on a tight schedule.

Kaziranga National Park: Elephants and Rhinos in Assam

Kaziranga, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in central Assam, is best known for harboring two-thirds of the world's one-horned Indian rhinoceros population. But the park also supports a substantial elephant population across its 430 square kilometers of tall grassland, marshes and dense tropical forest.

Jeep safaris through Kaziranga's four ranges — Kohora, Bagori, Agoratoli and Burapahar — offer encounters with elephant herds grazing in the grasslands. Sightings are less predictable than in the south, according to Lonely Planet, but the park's sheer density of megafauna makes every drive productive. The park opens from November to April, closing during the Assam monsoon when annual flooding replenishes the ecosystem.

Jim Corbett National Park: Elephants in the Himalayan Foothills

India's oldest national park, established in 1936 in the Uttarakhand foothills, combines sal forests, grasslands and riverine habitats along the Ramganga River. Corbett's elephant population is part of a broader northeastern corridor connecting Terai forests across the Indo-Gangetic plain.

Jeep safaris in the Bijrani and Dhikala zones offer the best chances. Dhikala, deep inside the park, requires an overnight stay in the forest rest house — a trade-off that rewards visitors with near-empty trails and uninterrupted wildlife encounters. The park operates from mid-November to mid-June.

Mudumalai and Wayanad: Completing the Nilgiri Circuit

Tamil Nadu's Mudumalai National Park and Kerala's Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary round out the Nilgiri Biosphere cluster. Mudumalai, nestled in the Nilgiri Hills, records one of the highest elephant densities in Asia at roughly 3.1 per square kilometer. Wayanad's Muthanga range is known for high elephant density and offers jeep safaris through tropical moist forest.

Together with Nagarhole and Bandipur, these four reserves form a contiguous habitat that allows elephants to migrate freely — a critical factor in the species' long-term viability. Tamil Nadu as a whole supports 3,136 elephants, the country's second-largest population after Karnataka.

Planning Your Visit

Most Indian wildlife reserves open between October and June, with the February-to-April dry season delivering peak sighting conditions. Safaris typically run at dawn and late afternoon, when animals are most active. Advance booking is essential at popular parks — Corbett's Dhikala zone and Bandipur's limited-entry safaris fill up months ahead during holiday periods.

For diaspora travelers combining a wildlife trip with family visits, the southern Nilgiri circuit is well connected from Bengaluru and Mysuru. Periyar is reachable from Kochi, and Kaziranga from Guwahati. Most parks offer a range of accommodation, from forest department rest houses to upscale safari lodges.
